Daniel visited a privately owned Christian bookstore that also sold engraved watches. He asked Lydia, the clerk, to see an expensive watch engraved with a Scripture verse. In conversation, Daniel falsely claimed to be Pastor Paul’s son. When Lydia handed him the watch, Daniel asked whether he could put it on, walk around the store to see how it felt, and then briefly step outside to view it in natural light. Lydia agreed, saying, “I know I can trust someone like you with the merchandise.”

Daniel walked out of the store wearing the watch and did not return. A week later, Lydia saw Daniel wearing the watch at a campus fellowship dinner. She told him that he must either pay for the watch or give it back. Daniel hissed, “You’ll be sorry if you mess with me.” Intimidated, Lydia backed off.

The following list of crimes is in descending order of seriousness. What is the most serious crime Daniel committed?

call: The following list of crimes is in descending order of seriousness. What is the most serious crime Daniel committed?
rightExplanation:
B is correct. Daniel committed larceny. He used a false present fact to get Lydia to hand him the watch for a limited try-on purpose. Lydia did not sell it to him, transfer ownership, or entrust it to him for an independent lawful purpose. Daniel then walked away with the watch.

Gold Key: In common-law theft labels, deception that gets possession only is larceny by trick; deception that gets title/ownership is false pretenses; lawful entrusted possession later converted is embezzlement; force or threat used in the taking is robbery.

Silver Key: Because the call says the crimes are listed in descending seriousness, test the top crime first. If robbery fails, move down the ladder and pick the most serious label that actually fits the taking.

studentScript: Robbery? No—the threat came later. False pretenses? No title. Embezzlement? No lawful entrustment. Possession-only trick plus walk-away: larceny.

A.signal: Threat fact exists, but it arrives after Daniel already walked away with the watch.
A.lawyer: Robbery would require force or threat as part of the taking; the later intimidation does not upgrade the earlier trick-taking.

B.signal: Daniel got limited possession by deception, walked away, and never received title.
B.lawyer: This is larceny by trick: possession obtained by deception without transfer of ownership.

C.signal: The lie matters, but the clerk did not sell or transfer ownership.
C.lawyer: False pretenses requires title/ownership obtained by misrepresentation; Daniel obtained only possession.

D.signal: Daniel was not an entrusted lawful possessor; he got the watch through a limited try-on deception.
D.lawyer: Embezzlement fits lawful possession followed by conversion, not possession obtained by trick.
